newsitem.title: UK: Study sees EMU sparking fund industry changes.
newsitem.headline: Study sees EMU sparking fund industry changes.

text.p: Increased competition under economic and monetary union (EMU) could result in major shifts in the European investment industry, with mergers and acquisitions and an increased niche focus likely, according to an industry study.
Investment advisers Frank Russell said smaller operators could narrow their product range, while other players may look to mergers and acquisitions or joint ventures to boost resources.

"With EMU and other factors leading to increased competition between investment firms in Europe, it will be more important than ever for managers to focus on the areas in which they have competitive advantages and to strengthen their resources in these areas," it said.
The study was based on a survey of over 100 institutional investment organisations in the UK, U.S., and across continental Europe.
It said firms recognised the need to add resources in cetain areas, but additional resources represented an entry barrier to many firms.
Other moves could include the outsourcing of management of some products to a third party.
The survey said regulations restricting cross-border investment on risk grounds would become increasingly unsustainable in coming years, and barriers to entry in the industry will rise.
"If firms are to appear credible as managers of Euro equity or fixed income portfolios, they will need to increase the resources they devote to analysing European markets, sectors and securities."
They will also have to strengthen sales teams if they are to successfully sell their services in new markets in Europe.

Larger firms can spread the cost of the investments over a greater asset volume and their unit costs will be largely unchanged, but smaller firms without the economies of scale of larger players will see unit costs rise and profitability fall.
Aside from EMU, managers must also prepare themselves for a shift to defined contribution pension schemes in some countries, requiring substantial investment in computer systems.

It said existing exit barriers would persist as organisations with strategic relationships between asset management and other businesses in which they are involved tending to remain in the industry even if they are not successful, as would firms that have stated their intention to remain or those that have bought investment companies.
Also, buyer power could be greater after EMU as some investors will be able to pool previously separate assets.

"Multinational companies with pension funds in several European countries may be able to rationalise their investment arrangements and appoint a much smaller group of firms to manage their domestic equity and fixed income assets," it said.
A trend to higher standards may further raise the ability of buyers to differentiate between investment products.
